<p id="S2.p12.7" class="ltx_p">so, for <math id="S2.p12.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> sufficiently large,
these are the Kähler forms of Kähler metrics
<math id="S2.p12.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p12.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math> defined on, say, the region <math id="S2.p12.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0&lt;t&lt;3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0&lt;t&lt;3</annotation></semantics></math>. Notice
that <math id="S2.p12.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is smooth across <math id="S2.p12.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math>, and that we have arranged for <math id="S2.p12.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.p12.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> to coincide when <math id="S2.p12.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>. Also observe that <math id="S2.p12.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> becomes
a genuine edge-cone metric on <math id="S2.p12.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> after making the coordinate change <math id="S2.p12.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta=(\beta\rho)^{1/\beta}e^{i\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ζ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta=(\beta\rho)^{1/\beta}e^{i\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. While one could
object that this coordinate change actually represents
a self-homeomorphism of <math id="S2.p12.m38" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> which is only smooth away from <math id="S2.p12.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>,
this is completely harmless for present purposes, since the relevant
curvature integrals will actually be performed on <math id="S2.p12.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M-\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M-\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p13.1" class="ltx_p">We now identify <math id="S2.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> with a tubular neighborhood
<math id="S2.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> via some diffeomorphism, and, for
any real number <math id="S2.p13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, we let <math id="S2.p13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{U}}_{T}\subset{\mathcal{U}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>⊂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{U}}_{T}\subset{\mathcal{U}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote
the closed tubular neighborhood
corresponding to the region <math id="S2.p13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\leq T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\leq T</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.p13.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>. We then use a cut-off function to extend <math id="S2.p13.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p13.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.p13.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>
as Riemannian metrics,
in such a way that they exactly agree on the complement of <math id="S2.p13.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{U}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{U}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>,
but are undamaged by the cut-off on <math id="S2.p13.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{U}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{U}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Calling these extensions
<math id="S2.p13.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p13.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, we then see that our basic desiderata have all been fulfilled:
<math id="S2.p13.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is an edge-cone metric of cone angle <math id="S2.p13.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S2.p13.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p13.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is a smooth
Riemannian metric on <math id="S2.p13.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, both are Kähler on a tubular neighborhood
<math id="S2.p13.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{V}}=\Int{\mathcal{U}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Int </mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{V}}=\Int{\mathcal{U}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.p13.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, and the two metrics agree on the complement of
a smaller tubular neighborhood <math id="S2.p13.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{U}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{U}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.p13.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p14" class="ltx_para">

<p id="S2.p14.3" class="ltx_p">is defined in terms of the ratio <math id="S2.p14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V/V_{0}=d\mu_{g}/d\mu_{g_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V/V_{0}=d\mu_{g}/d\mu_{g_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math> of the volume forms of <math id="S2.p14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p14.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus</p>

the outward pointing orientation
relative to <math id="S2.p14.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, relative to

along the <math id="S2.p14.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ζ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta</annotation></semantics></math>-axis, the volume forms of <math id="S2.p14.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p14.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> are
represented by the component functions</p>

Restricting this to <math id="S2.p14.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>ϵ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math>, then along
the <math id="S2.p14.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ζ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta</annotation></semantics></math>-axis this expression is just</p>
<table id="S2.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_eqnarray ltx_eqn_table">

<p id="S2.p14.12" class="ltx_p">since <math id="S2.p14.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varrho_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϱ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varrho_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is smooth across <math id="S2.p14.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and is invariant under the action of

<p id="S2.p14.13" class="ltx_p">by virtue of (<a href="#S2.E20" title="In 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.20</span></a>).
But since <math id="S2.p14.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varrho_{0}/2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϱ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varrho_{0}/2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> represents <math id="S2.p14.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}(T^{1,0}E)=c_{1}(T^{1,0}\Sigma)+c_{1}(E)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{1}(T^{1,0}E)=c_{1}(T^{1,0}\Sigma)+c_{1}(E)</annotation></semantics></math> in deRham cohomology, and since <math id="S2.p14.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}(E)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo id="S2.p14.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\alpha/2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" <p id="S2.p14.16" class="ltx_p">which is exactly the sought-after identity (<a href="#S2.E8" title="In 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.8</span></a>) for the particular metrics <math id="S2.p14.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p14.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Applying the Gauss-Bonnet and signature fomulæ to the smooth metric <math id="S2.p14.m41" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>
now transforms
(<a href="#S2.E22" title="In 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.22</span></a>) into</p>

<p id="S2.p14.17" class="ltx_p">which is exactly (<a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>), with defect <math id="S2.p14.m42" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dft_{+}(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>def</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dft_{+}(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> given by (<a href="#S2.E5" title="In 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>).
 <span id="S2.p14.17.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-2.0pt;"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:7.0pt;height:8.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span></span>

<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Theorems <a href="#S2.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> and <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> now follow.
Indeed, given any <math id="S2.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>,
Proposition <a href="#S2.Thmprop1" title="Proposition 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> shows that (<a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>) holds for some edge-cone
metric <math id="S2.p15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S2.p15.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> of cone angle <math id="S2.p15.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, and Lemma <a href="#S2.Thmlem1" title="Lemma 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> thus shows
that the same is true of any edge-cone metric on any <math id="S2.p15.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> for any <math id="S2.p15.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>.
Applying this conclusion to the
orientation-reversed manifold <math id="S2.p15.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{M}</annotation></semantics></math> shows that (<a href="#S2.E4" title="In 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>) also holds, and
taking appropriate linear combinations then proves
Theorems <a href="#S2.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> and <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p16.1" class="ltx_p">So far, we have assumed that <math id="S2.p16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is oriented, but this is not essential.
Of course, (<a href="#S2.E1" title="In Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>) makes perfectly good sense even
if <math id="S2.p16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is non-orientable, but more must be said about
(<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>).
As long as <math id="S2.p16.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is oriented, the Euler number of the normal bundle of <math id="S2.p16.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset M</annotation></semantics></math>
will have the twisted coefficients needed to be consistently integrated on <math id="S2.p16.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>,
and this normal bundle will therefore have
a well-defined Euler number which counts the zeroes, with multiplicities,
of a generic section. When <math id="S2.p16.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset M</annotation></semantics></math> is non-orientable, we now decree that
<math id="S2.p16.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\Sigma]^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\Sigma]^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is to be interpreted in
(<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) as meaning
the Euler number of its normal bundle
rather than being defined in terms of homology classes on <math id="S2.p16.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.
Now this Euler number can be calculated by passing to an oriented double cover of
<math id="S2.p16.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, integrating the Euler class of the pull-back, and then dividing by <math id="S2.p16.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>;
meanwhile, the correction term
in (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) is represented by an integral supported in a
tubular neighborhood of <math id="S2.p16.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, so one can similarly compute it by
passing to a double cover of a tubular neighborhood of
<math id="S2.p16.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and then dividing by <math id="S2.p16.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>. This covering trick allows us to prove
Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> even when <math id="S2.p16.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is non-orientable,
and Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> even if neither <math id="S2.p16.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> nor <math id="S2.p16.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is orientable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p17.1" class="ltx_p">This observation has a useful corollary.
Suppose that <math id="S2.p17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> admits an almost-complex structure
<math id="S2.p17.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> and that <math id="S2.p17.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset M</annotation></semantics></math> is totally real with respect to <math id="S2.p17.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>,
in the sense that <math id="S2.p17.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\Sigma\cap J(T\Sigma)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><mo>∩</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\Sigma\cap J(T\Sigma)=0</annotation></semantics></math> at every point of <math id="S2.p17.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.
We now give <math id="S2.p17.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> the orientation induced by <math id="S2.p17.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>, but emphasize that
<math id="S2.p17.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> might not even be orientable. If <math id="S2.p17.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{1},e_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{1},e_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is a basis <math id="S2.p17.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> at some point,
we now observe that <math id="S2.p17.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(e_{1},e_{2},Je_{1},Je_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(e_{1},e_{2},Je_{1},Je_{2})</annotation></semantics></math> is then a <span id="S2.p17.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reverse-oriented</span>
basis for <math id="S2.p17.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="TM" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">TM</annotation></semantics></math>. Under these circumstances,
the Euler number of the normal bundle of <math id="S2.p17.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>,
in the sense discussed above, therefore equals <math id="S2.p17.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\chi(\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\chi(\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>. In light of our previous
remarks, we thus obtain a close cousin of Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmprop2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_prop">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmprop2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2.2</span></span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmprop2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,J)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,J)</annotation></semantics></math> be an almost-complex <math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold, equipped with
the orientation induced by <math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>,
and let
<math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset M</annotation></semantics></math> be a (possibly non-orientable) surface which
is totally real with respect to <math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, for any edge-cone metric <math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>
of cone angle <math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S2.Thmprop2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S2.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(M)+\frac{1}{3}(1-\beta^{2})\chi(\Sigma)=\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{M}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)d\mu~." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mi>M</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.330em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(M)+\frac{1}{3}(1-\beta^{2})\chi(\Sigma)=\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{M}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)d\mu~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2.23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Indices and Orbifolds</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the calculations used in §<a href="#S2" title="2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> suffice to
prove Theorems <a href="#S2.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> and <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>,
they hardly provide a transparent explanation of
the detailed structure of equations
(<a href="#S2.E1" title="In Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>) and (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>).
In this section, we will describe another method for obtaining
these formulæ that makes the edge-cone corrections seem
a great deal less mysterious. For brevity and clarity, we will
confine ourselves to providing a second proof of Theorem
<a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>. The same method can also be used to prove Theorem
<a href="#S2.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>, but several more elementary proofs are also possible in this case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our approach is based on
the <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-index theorem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, so we begin by recalling
what this tells us about the signature operator in four dimensions.
If a finite group <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>
acts on a compact oriented connected <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>, we can choose a
<math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-invariant decomposition</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(M,{\mathbb{R}})=H^{+}\oplus H^{-}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>⊕</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(M,{\mathbb{R}})=H^{+}\oplus H^{-}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">of the second cohomology into subspaces on which the intersection form
is positive- and negative-definite; for example, we could equip <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> with
a <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-invariant Riemannian metric <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{g}</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{\pm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>±</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{\pm}</annotation></semantics></math> consist of those
de Rham classes which
self-dual or anti-self-dual harmonic representatives, respectively, with respect to this metric.
For each <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}\in\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}\in\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>,
we then let <math id="S3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}_{*}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the induced action of <math id="S3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})</annotation></semantics></math>, and
set</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau({\zap g},X)=\tr({\zap g}_{*}|_{H^{+}})-\tr({\zap g}_{*}|_{H^{-}})~." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msub><mo rspace="0.052em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau({\zap g},X)=\tr({\zap g}_{*}|_{H^{+}})-\tr({\zap g}_{*}|_{H^{-}})~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">In particular, <math id="S3.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(1,X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(1,X)</annotation></semantics></math> coincides with the usual signature <math id="S3.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(X)</annotation></semantics></math>.
By contrast, when <math id="S3.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}\neq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}\neq 1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau({\zap g},X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau({\zap g},X)</annotation></semantics></math>
is instead expressible in terms of the fixed-point set <math id="S3.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S3.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math>.
To do this, we first express <math id="S3.p2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> as a disjoint union of isolated fixed points <math id="S3.p2.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>
and compact surfaces <math id="S3.p2.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\Sigma}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\Sigma}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>; at each <math id="S3.p2.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\Sigma}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\Sigma}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>,
<math id="S3.p2.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> then
acts by rotating the normal bundle through some angle <math id="S3.p2.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϑ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas
at each isolated fixed point <math id="S3.p2.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p2.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> acts on <math id="S3.p2.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{x_{j}}X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{x_{j}}X</annotation></semantics></math> by rotating
through angles <math id="S3.p2.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> in a pair of orthogonal <math id="S3.p2.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-planes.
With these conventions, the <math id="S3.p2.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional case of the relevant fixed-point formula <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, Proposition (6.12)]</cite>
becomes</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="S3.p2.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p2.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> respectively run over the <math id="S3.p2.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>- and <math id="S3.p2.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional components
of the fixed-point set <math id="S3.p2.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> denote the orbifold <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X/\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X/\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, and
notice that
the <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-invariant
subspace <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})^{\mathbf{G}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝐆</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})^{\mathbf{G}}</annotation></semantics></math>
of <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})</annotation></semantics></math> can be identified with
<math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(M,{\mathbb{R}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(M,{\mathbb{R}})</annotation></semantics></math>
via pull-back. Since</p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{|\mathbf{G}|}\sum_{{\zap g}\in\mathbf{G}}{\zap g}_{*}:H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})\to H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})^{\mathbf{G}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>𝐆</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝐆</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{|\mathbf{G}|}\sum_{{\zap g}\in\mathbf{G}}{\zap g}_{*}:H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})\to H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}})^{\mathbf{G}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">is the <math id="S3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-invariant projection,
and since the cup product commutes with pull-backs,
we therefore have</p>

</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We now specialize our discussion by assuming
that the action has a fixed point, but that no fixed point is isolated.
Thus, if <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}\neq\{1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐆</mi><mo>≠</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}\neq\{1\}</annotation></semantics></math>,
there must be at least one
fixed surface <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\Sigma}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\Sigma}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the induced action on the normal bundle of each
such <math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\Sigma}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\Sigma}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> must be
effective. Hence
<math id="S3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}={\mathbb{Z}}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐆</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}={\mathbb{Z}}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> for some positive integer <math id="S3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. Moreover,
for each <math id="S3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, the exponentials <math id="S3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{i\vartheta_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ϑ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{i\vartheta_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math>
of the rotation angles <math id="S3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϑ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> appearing in (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>)
must sweep through all the <math id="S3.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p^{\rm th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>th</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p^{\rm th}</annotation></semantics></math> roots of unity as
<math id="S3.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> runs through <math id="S3.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We can therefore rewrite (<a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>) as</p>
<table id="S3.EGx9" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_eqnarray ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tau(M)=\frac{1}{p}\left[\tau(X)+\left(\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\csc^{2}\left[\frac{k\pi}{p}\right]\right)[\hat{\Sigma}]^{2}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>p</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><msup><mi>csc</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\tau(M)=\frac{1}{p}\left[\tau(X)+\left(\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\csc^{2}\left[\frac{k\pi}{p}\right]\right)[\hat{\Sigma}]^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3.3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p4.m12" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{\Sigma}=X^{\mathbf{G}}=\cup_{k}\hat{\Sigma}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>X</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>𝐆</mi></msup><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">∪</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\Sigma}=X^{\mathbf{G}}=\cup_{k}\hat{\Sigma}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>.
On the other hand, as pointed out by Hirzebruch <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, §4]</cite>, the
trigonometric sum in (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) has an algebraic simplification</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\csc^{2}\left(\frac{k\pi}{p}\right)=\frac{p^{2}-1}{3}~," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msup><mi>csc</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0.330em">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\csc^{2}\left(\frac{k\pi}{p}\right)=\frac{p^{2}-1}{3}~,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3.4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p4.3" class="ltx_p">as can be proved using the
the Cauchy residue theorem.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Now since <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}}=\hat{\Sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msup><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}}=\hat{\Sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> has been assumed to be purely of codimension <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>,
<math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=X/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=X/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is a manifold, and comes equipped with a surface
<math id="S3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset M</annotation></semantics></math> which is the image of <math id="S3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\Sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\Sigma}</annotation></semantics></math>. Observe,
moreover, that <math id="S3.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\Sigma]^{2}=p[\hat{\Sigma}]^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\Sigma]^{2}=p[\hat{\Sigma}]^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Substituting (<a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>) into (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) therefore yields</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(M)-\frac{1}{3}(1-p^{-2})[\Sigma]^{2}=\frac{1}{p}\tau(X)~." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>p</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.052em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(M)-\frac{1}{3}(1-p^{-2})[\Sigma]^{2}=\frac{1}{p}\tau(X)~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3.5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">However, the usual signature theorem tells us that
<math id="S3.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(X)=\frac{1}{3}\int_{X}p_{1}(TX)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(X)=\frac{1}{3}\int_{X}p_{1}(TX)</annotation></semantics></math>, and this allows us
to rewrite the right-hand side of (<a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>) as</p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\frac{1}{p}\cdot\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{X}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{\hat{g}}d\mu_{\hat{g}}=\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{M}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{g}d\mu_{g}" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><msup><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>μ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{p}\cdot\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{X}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{\hat{g}}d\mu_{\hat{g}}=\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{M}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{g}d\mu_{g}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p5.3" class="ltx_p">because <math id="S3.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X-\hat{\Sigma},\hat{g})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X-\hat{\Sigma},\hat{g})</annotation></semantics></math> is a <math id="S3.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-sheeted cover of <math id="S3.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M-\Sigma,g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M-\Sigma,g)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Since <math id="S3.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is an edge-cone metric on <math id="S3.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1/p</annotation></semantics></math>,
we have therefore obtained a quite different proof of (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) in this special case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The global quotients with <math id="S3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1/p</annotation></semantics></math> we have just analyzed
constitute a special class of
orbifolds. Without recourse to the results in the previous section,
one can similarly show that Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> also applies
to arbitrary orbifolds with singular set of pure codimension <math id="S3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> and cone angle <math id="S3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi/p</annotation></semantics></math>,
even when the spaces in question are not global quotients.
As is explained in
Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Appendix ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, the
best way of proving this
involves the Index Theorem for transversely elliptic operators, and
also yields results in higher dimensions.
We will now assume this more general fact,and see how it leads to a
different proof of Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To do so, we revisit the global quotients discussed above, but now turn the
picture upside down by letting
<math id="S3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> play the role previously assigned to <math id="S3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>. That is, we now assume that
there is an effective action of <math id="S3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> with fixed point set
<math id="S3.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, and set <math id="S3.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y=M/{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y=M/{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S3.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varpi:M\to Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϖ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varpi:M\to Y</annotation></semantics></math>
be the quotient map, and let
<math id="S3.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\check{\Sigma}=\varpi(\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϖ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\check{\Sigma}=\varpi(\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Chose an orbifold metric <math id="S3.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\check{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\check{g}</annotation></semantics></math>
of cone angle <math id="S3.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi/p</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Y,\check{\Sigma})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Y,\check{\Sigma})</annotation></semantics></math>, and assume, per the
above discussion, that
(<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) is already
known to hold for orbifolds. Our previous argument tells us that</p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(Y)=\frac{1}{q}\tau(M)+\frac{1}{3}(1-q^{-2})~[\check{\Sigma}]^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>q</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.330em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(Y)=\frac{1}{q}\tau(M)+\frac{1}{3}(1-q^{-2})~[\check{\Sigma}]^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p7.2" class="ltx_p">while we also have the formula</p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
