<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(Y)=\frac{1}{3}(1-p^{-2})[\check{\Sigma}]^{2}+\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{Y}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{\check{g}}d\mu_{\check{g}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mi>Y</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(Y)=\frac{1}{3}(1-p^{-2})[\check{\Sigma}]^{2}+\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{Y}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{\check{g}}d\mu_{\check{g}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p7.3" class="ltx_p">by assumption.
Remembering that <math id="S3.p7.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\check{\Sigma}]^{2}=q[\Sigma]^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\check{\Sigma}]^{2}=q[\Sigma]^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, we therefore obtain</p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\tau(Y)-\frac{1}{3}\left(1-\left[\frac{q}{p}\right]^{2}\right)[{\Sigma}]^{2}=q\cdot\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{Y}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{\check{g}}d\mu_{\check{g}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mi>p</mi></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mi>Y</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><msup><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover></msub><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>μ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(Y)-\frac{1}{3}\left(1-\left[\frac{q}{p}\right]^{2}\right)[{\Sigma}]^{2}=q\cdot\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{Y}\left(|W_{+}|^{2}-|W_{-}|^{2}\right)_{\check{g}}d\mu_{\check{g}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p7.4" class="ltx_p">by straightforward algebraic manipulation.
Reinterpreting the right-hand side as a curvature integral on <math id="S3.p7.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> for the
edge cone metric <math id="S3.p7.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=\varpi^{*}\check{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ϖ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=\varpi^{*}\check{g}</annotation></semantics></math>, we thus deduce
(<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) for this large class of examples
where <math id="S3.p7.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=q/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=q/p</annotation></semantics></math> is an arbitrary positive rational number.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We now consider the general case of
Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>
with <math id="S3.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=q/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=q/p</annotation></semantics></math> rational. First, notice that
the same elementary trick used in §<a href="#S2" title="2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that the
the <math id="S3.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>-dependent correction term in (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>)
can be localized to a neighborhood of <math id="S3.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. Moreover,
this correction term is additive
under disjoint unions, and multiplicative under covers.
Moreover, Lemma
<a href="#S2.Thmlem1" title="Lemma 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> shows that they are independent of the particular choice of metric,
so we may assume that the given edge-cone metric of cone angle <math id="S3.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi q/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi q/p</annotation></semantics></math>
is rotationally invariant
on a tubular neighborhood of <math id="S3.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.
Cut out such a tubular neighborhood <math id="S3.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math>
of <math id="S3.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, and consider the isometric <math id="S3.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>-action corresponding to
rotation in the normal bundle of <math id="S3.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> though an angle of <math id="S3.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi/q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi/q</annotation></semantics></math>.
We then have an induced <span id="S3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">free</span> action on the oriented <math id="S3.p8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold
<math id="S3.p8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math>. However, the cobordism group for free <math id="S3.p8.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>-actions is of
finite order in any odd dimension <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. Thus, there is an
oriented <math id="S3.p8.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold-with-boundary <math id="S3.p8.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> with free <math id="S3.p8.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>-action,
where <math id="S3.p8.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial Z</annotation></semantics></math> is
disjoint union of, say, <math id="S3.p8.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> copies of <math id="S3.p8.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math>, each equipped with the original
<math id="S3.p8.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>-action. Let <math id="S3.p8.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{M}</annotation></semantics></math> then be obtained from the reverse-oriented manifold
<math id="S3.p8.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> by capping off each of its <math id="S3.p8.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> boundary components with a copy of
<math id="S3.p8.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math>, and notice that, by construction, <math id="S3.p8.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{M}</annotation></semantics></math> comes equipped
with a <math id="S3.p8.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>-action whose fixed-point set consists of <math id="S3.p8.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> copies of <math id="S3.p8.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.
We extend <math id="S3.p8.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> copies of the given edge-cone metric <math id="S3.p8.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.p8.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math> to a
<math id="S3.p8.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>-invariant metric <math id="S3.p8.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.p8.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{M}</annotation></semantics></math>. However,
<math id="S3.p8.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y=\tilde{M}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y=\tilde{M}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> is now a manifold, and <math id="S3.p8.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> pushes down
to <math id="S3.p8.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> as an orbifold metric <math id="S3.p8.m38" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\check{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\check{g}</annotation></semantics></math> of cone angle <math id="S3.p8.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi/p</annotation></semantics></math>.
Our previous argument for global quotients then shows that
(<a href="#S2.E1" title="In Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>) and (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) hold for <math id="S3.p8.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Z,\coprod_{1}^{\ell}\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∐</mo><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Z,\coprod_{1}^{\ell}\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>,
and additivity therefore shows that the correction terms are as promised
for each of the <math id="S3.p8.m41" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> identical copies of <math id="S3.p8.m42" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math>. This shows that
(<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) holds for any edge-cone manifold of cone angle <math id="S3.p8.m43" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, provided
that <math id="S3.p8.m44" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is a positive rational number <math id="S3.p8.m45" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q/p</annotation></semantics></math>. Multiplicativity
of the correction
under covers similarly allows one to drop the assumption that <math id="S3.p8.m46" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is orientable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, an elementary continuity argument allows us to extend our formula from
rational to real <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>. Consider a smooth family
of edge-cone metrics on <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(2)</annotation></semantics></math> symmetry about <math id="S3.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, but with
cone angle varying over the entire positive reals <math id="S3.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The left- and right-hand sides of (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) then vary
continuously as <math id="S3.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> varies, and their difference vanishes for
<math id="S3.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{+}\cap\mathbb{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>∩</mo><mi>ℚ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{+}\cap\mathbb{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>. By continuity, the two sides therefore agree for all <math id="S3.p9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>.
With the help of Lemma <a href="#S2.Thmlem1" title="Lemma 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>, this gives us alternative proofs of
Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> and Proposition <a href="#S2.Thmprop2" title="Proposition 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Edges and Einstein Metrics</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As we saw in §<a href="#S2" title="2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, Theorems <a href="#S2.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> and <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> are equivalent to
the fact that every edge-cone metric <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> of cone angle <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies</p>
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi\pm 3\tau)(M)-\dft_{\pm}(\Sigma,\beta)=\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\int_{M}\left[\frac{s^{2}}{24}+2|W_{\pm}|^{2}-\frac{|\mathring{r}|^{2}}{2}\right]_{g}d\mu_{g}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>def</mi><mo>±</mo></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mi>M</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>24</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>±</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>̊</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mi>g</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi\pm 3\tau)(M)-\dft_{\pm}(\Sigma,\beta)=\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\int_{M}\left[\frac{s^{2}}{24}+2|W_{\pm}|^{2}-\frac{|\mathring{r}|^{2}}{2}\right]_{g}d\mu_{g}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">for both choices of the <math id="S4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> sign, where</p>
<table id="S4.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dft_{\pm}(\Sigma,\beta)=2(1-\beta)\chi(\Sigma)\pm(1-\beta^{2})[\Sigma]^{2}~." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>def</mi><mo>±</mo></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dft_{\pm}(\Sigma,\beta)=2(1-\beta)\chi(\Sigma)\pm(1-\beta^{2})[\Sigma]^{2}~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p1.3" class="ltx_p">However, if the edge-cone metric <math id="S4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is Einstein, it then satisfies <math id="S4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathring{r}\equiv 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>̊</mo></mover><mo>≡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathring{r}\equiv 0</annotation></semantics></math>,
and the integrand on the right-hand-side of (<a href="#S4.E1" title="In 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>) is consequently non-negative.
The existence of an Einstein edge-cone metric of cone angle <math id="S4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math> on
<math id="S4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> therefore implies the topological constraints
that</p>
<table id="S4.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi\pm 3\tau)(M)\geq\dft_{\pm}(\Sigma,\beta)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>def</mi><mo>±</mo></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi\pm 3\tau)(M)\geq\dft_{\pm}(\Sigma,\beta)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p1.4" class="ltx_p">and equality can occur for a given choice of sign only if the Einstein metric
satisfies <math id="S4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\equiv 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>≡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\equiv 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\pm}\equiv 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>±</mo></msub><mo>≡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\pm}\equiv 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Since the metric
in question also satisfies <math id="S4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathring{r}\equiv 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>̊</mo></mover><mo>≡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathring{r}\equiv 0</annotation></semantics></math> by hypothesis, equality only occurs if
<math id="S4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda^{\pm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>±</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda^{\pm}</annotation></semantics></math> is flat, which is to say that the metric in question
is locally hyper-Kähler, in a manner compatible with the <math id="S4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math>-orientation of <math id="S4.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.
This proves a more refined version of Theorem <a href="#Thmmain1" title="Theorem A ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmthm1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_thm">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmthm1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 4.1</span></span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmthm1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> be a smooth compact <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold, and let <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset M</annotation></semantics></math> be a
compact orientable embedded surface. If <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> admits
an Einstein edge-cone metric of cone angle <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math>,
then <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> must satisfy the inequalities</span></p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\geq(1-\beta)\left[2\chi(\Sigma)+(1+\beta)[\Sigma]^{2}\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\geq(1-\beta)\left[2\chi(\Sigma)+(1+\beta)[\Sigma]^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">and</span></p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi-3\tau)(M)\geq(1-\beta)\left[2\chi(\Sigma)-(1+\beta)[\Sigma]^{2}\right]~." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.052em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi-3\tau)(M)\geq(1-\beta)\left[2\chi(\Sigma)-(1+\beta)[\Sigma]^{2}\right]~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Moreover, equality occurs in (<a href="#S4.E2" title="In Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) if and only if <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is locally hyper-Kähler,
in a manner compatible with the given orientation of <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>. Similarly,
equality occurs in (<a href="#S4.E3" title="In Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) if and only if <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is locally hyper-Kähler,
in a manner compatible with the opposite orientation of <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recall that
a Riemannian
<math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold is locally hyper-Kähler iff it
is Ricci-flat and locally Kähler. Brendle’s recent construction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>
of Ricci-flat Kähler manifolds with edge-cone singularities of small cone angle
thus provides an interesting class of examples which saturate inequality (<a href="#S4.E2" title="In Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As a related illustration of the meaning of Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>, let us now consider
what happens when the cone angle tends to zero.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmthm2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_cor">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmthm2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 4.2</span></span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmthm2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> admits
a sequence <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> of Einstein edge-cone metrics with cone angles <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta_{j}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta_{j}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>,
then <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> must satisfy the two inequalities</span></p>
<table id="S4.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi\pm 3\tau)(M)\geq 2\chi(\Sigma)\pm[\Sigma]^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>±</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi\pm 3\tau)(M)\geq 2\chi(\Sigma)\pm[\Sigma]^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">with equality for a given sign iff the <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norms of both <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\pm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>±</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\pm}</annotation></semantics></math> tend to zero
as <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For example, let <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> be a smooth cubic curve, and
let <math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> be obtained from <math id="S4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> by blowing up <math id="S4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> points
which do not lie on <math id="S4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. Considering <math id="S4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> as
a submanifold of <math id="S4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, we always have <math id="S4.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\chi(\Sigma)+[\Sigma]^{2}=0+3^{2}=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\chi(\Sigma)+[\Sigma]^{2}=0+3^{2}=9</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas
<math id="S4.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi+3\tau)(M)=(2\chi+3\tau)({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2})-k=9-k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi+3\tau)(M)=(2\chi+3\tau)({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2})-k=9-k</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus,
<math id="S4.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> does not admit Einstein metrics of small cone angle
when <math id="S4.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is a positive integer. By contrast,
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> leads one to believe that <math id="S4.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">should</span>
admit Einstein metrics of small cone angle, and that,
as the angle tends to zero, these should tend to
previously discovered hyper-Kähler metrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
This would nicely illustrate the boundary case of Corollary <a href="#S4.Thmthm2" title="Corollary 4.2 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">While many interesting results have recently been obtained
about the Kähler case of Einstein
edge metrics with <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in(0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in(0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, the large cone-angle regime of the problem seems
technically
intractable. It is thus interesting to observe Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> gives us strong
obstructions to the existence of Einstein edge-cone metrics with large cone angle,
even without imposing the Kähler condition. Indeed, first notice that
dividing (<a href="#S4.E2" title="In Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) and (<a href="#S4.E3" title="In Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) by <math id="S4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and taking the limit as
<math id="S4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> yields the inequalities</p>
<table id="S4.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\geq-[\Sigma]^{2}\mbox{ and }0\geq[\Sigma]^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> and </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\geq-[\Sigma]^{2}\mbox{ and }0\geq[\Sigma]^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p5.2" class="ltx_p">so that existence is obstructed for large <math id="S4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> unless <math id="S4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\Sigma]^{2}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\Sigma]^{2}=0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Similarly, dividing the sum of (<a href="#S4.E2" title="In Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) and (<a href="#S4.E3" title="In Theorem 4.1 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) by <math id="S4.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\beta</annotation></semantics></math>
and letting <math id="S4.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> yields</p>
<table id="S4.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\geq-\chi(\Sigma)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\geq-\chi(\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p5.3" class="ltx_p">so existence for large <math id="S4.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is obstructed in most cases:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmthm3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_cor">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmthm3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 4.3</span></span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmthm3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose that <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\subset M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\subset M</annotation></semantics></math> is a
connected
oriented surface with either non-zero self-intersection or
genus <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 2</annotation></semantics></math>. Then there is a real number <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> such that
<math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> does not admit Einstein edge-cone metrics of cone angle
<math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math> for any <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\geq\beta_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\geq\beta_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Of course,
this result does not provide obstructions in all cases, and examples show that
this is inevitable. For example, consider an equatorial <math id="S4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-sphere
<math id="S4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}\subset S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}\subset S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math> is thought of as the unit sphere in <math id="S4.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{5}={\mathbb{R}}^{3}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{5}={\mathbb{R}}^{3}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, we make take our <math id="S4.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the inverse image of the origin under projection to
<math id="S4.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. By taking polar coordinates on this <math id="S4.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, we can thus identify <math id="S4.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}-S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}-S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> with
<math id="S4.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Rotating in the circle factor then gives us a Killing field on <math id="S4.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, and there
is an interesting conformal rescaling of the standard metric obtained by requiring
that this conformal Killing field have unit length in the new metric. What we
obtain in this way is a conformal equivalence between <math id="S4.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}-S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}-S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
and the Riemannian product <math id="S4.p6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}^{3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. More precisely,
the standard metric on <math id="S4.p6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math> now becomes</p>
<table id="S4.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\sech^{2}\text{ya})[h+d\theta^{2}]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>sech </mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mtext>ya</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sech^{2}\text{ya})[h+d\theta^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.p6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is the standard curvature <math id="S4.p6.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> metric on <math id="S4.p6.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, and where
<math id="S4.p6.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{ya}:\mathcal{H}^{3}\to{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>ya</mtext><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{ya}:\mathcal{H}^{3}\to{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the distance in <math id="S4.p6.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> from some arbitrary
base-point. By a minor alteration, we then obtain the family</p>
<table id="S4.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=(\sech^{2}\text{ya})[h+\beta^{2}d\theta^{2}]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>sech </mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mtext>ya</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=(\sech^{2}\text{ya})[h+\beta^{2}d\theta^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p6.3" class="ltx_p">of edge-cone metrics on <math id="S4.p6.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math> with arbitrary cone angle <math id="S4.p6.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math>. By setting
<math id="S4.p6.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\theta}=\beta\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\theta}=\beta\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, we see that these edge-cone metrics are actually locally
isometric to the standard metric on <math id="S4.p6.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so, in particular, are all Einstein;
in other words, these edge-cone metrics are simply obtained by passing to the universal cover
<math id="S4.p6.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{3}\times{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{3}\times{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.p6.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}-S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}-S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and then dividing out by some arbitrary translation of
the <math id="S4.p6.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℝ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> factor.
Since this works for any <math id="S4.p6.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, we see that it is inevitable that
Corollary <a href="#S4.Thmthm3" title="Corollary 4.3 ‣ 4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> does not apply to genus zero surfaces of trivial self-intersection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The above edge-cone metrics <math id="S4.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> can be obtained from the family</p>
<table id="S4.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}=\beta^{-1}h+\beta~d\theta^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.330em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}=\beta^{-1}h+\beta~d\theta^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p7.2" class="ltx_p">by a suitable conformal rescaling. In the next section,
we will see that this can be interestingly generalized by replacing the
constant function <math id="S4.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V=\beta^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V=\beta^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> with a harmonic function, and
by replacing the flat circle bundle <math id="S4.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{H}}^{3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{H}}^{3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> with
a principal <math id="S4.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{U}}(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{U}}(1)</annotation></semantics></math>-bundle over <math id="S4.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{H}}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{H}}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> which is equipped with a connection whose curvature is the closed <math id="S4.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-form
<math id="S4.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\star dV" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋆</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\star dV</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Edges and Instantons</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we will study families of self-dual edge-cone metrics
on <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds, and observe that these metrics
are interestingly related to certain gravitational instantons.
For our purposes, a gravitational instanton will mean a complete non-compact
Ricci-flat Riemannian <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold which is both simply connected and self-dual,
in the sense that
<math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{-}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{-}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that such spaces are necessarily hyper-Kähler, but that the orientation
we will give them here is opposite the one induced by the hyper-Kähler structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As indicated at the end of §<a href="#S4" title="4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we will
begin by considering a construction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, called the <span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hyperbolic ansatz</span>,
that builds explicit self-dual conformal metrics out of positive harmonic functions on
regions of hyperbolic <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-space. To this end, let
<math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{U}}\subset{\mathcal{H}}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{U}}\subset{\mathcal{H}}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> be an open set in hyperbolic <math id="S5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-space,
and let <math id="S5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V:{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V:{\mathcal{U}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> be a function which is harmonic with respect
to the hyperbolic metric <math id="S5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>. The <math id="S5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-form <math id="S5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\star dV" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋆</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\star dV</annotation></semantics></math> is then closed, and
we will furthermore suppose that the deRham class <math id="S5.p2.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="[(\star dV)/2\pi]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">⋆</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[(\star dV)/2\pi]</annotation></semantics></math>
represents an integer class in <math id="S5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}({\mathcal{U}},{\mathbb{R}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}({\mathcal{U}},{\mathbb{R}})</annotation></semantics></math>. The theory of Chern classes
then guarantees that there is a principal <math id="S5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}(1)</annotation></semantics></math>-bundle <math id="S5.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{P}}\to{\mathcal{U}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{P}}\to{\mathcal{U}}</annotation></semantics></math>
