which carries connection <math id="S5.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>-form <math id="S5.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> of curvature
<math id="S5.p2.m14" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="d\Theta=\star dV" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">⋆</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\Theta=\star dV</annotation></semantics></math>. We may then consider the Riemannian metric</p>
<table id="S5.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}=Vh+V^{-1}\Theta^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}=Vh+V^{-1}\Theta^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5.1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p2.2" class="ltx_p">on the total space <math id="S5.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math> of our circle bundle. Remarkably, this metric
is automatically self-dual with respect to a standard orientation of <math id="S5.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{P}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{P}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Since this last condition, that <math id="S5.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{-}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{-}=0</annotation></semantics></math>, is conformally invariant, multiplying
<math id="S5.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> by any positive conformal factor will result in another self-dual metric.
For shrewd choices of <math id="S5.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> and the conformal factor, interesting
compact self-dual edge-cone manifolds can be constructed in this way. Indeed,
one can even sometimes arrange for the resulting edge-cone metric to also be Einstein.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We already considered the case of constant <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> at the end of §<a href="#S4" title="4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
To obtain something more interesting, we now choose our potential to be</p>
<table id="S5.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V=\beta^{-1}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{p_{j}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>G</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V=\beta^{-1}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{p_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5.2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is an arbitrary positive constant,
<math id="S5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\in{\mathcal{H}}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\in{\mathcal{H}}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> are distinct points in hyperbolic <math id="S5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-space,
and where <math id="S5.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{p_{j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{p_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the corresponding Green’s functions.
For simplicity, we will use the same conformal rescaling</p>
<table id="S5.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p3.3" class="ltx_p">that was used in §<a href="#S4" title="4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, where <span id="S5.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">ya</span> denotes the distance from some arbitrary
base-point in <math id="S5.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. The metric-space completion
<math id="S5.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\mathcal{P}\cup\Sigma\cup\{\hat{p}_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\mathcal{P}\cup\Sigma\cup\{\hat{p}_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math>
of
<math id="S5.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{P},g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{P},g)</annotation></semantics></math> then carries a natural smooth structure making it diffeomorphic to
the connected sum</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="S5.p3.4" class="ltx_p">and
<math id="S5.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> then extends to <math id="S5.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>
as an edge-cone metric
with cone angle <math id="S5.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math> along a surface <math id="S5.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\approx S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>≈</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\approx S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
of self-intersection <math id="S5.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>. Indeed, <math id="S5.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1</annotation></semantics></math>,
this exactly reproduces the self-dual metics on <math id="S5.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> constructed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>.
For general <math id="S5.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, the picture is essentially the same; metric-space completion
adds one point <math id="S5.p3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> for each of the base-points <math id="S5.p3.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a <math id="S5.p3.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-sphere <math id="S5.p3.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding
to the <math id="S5.p3.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-sphere at infinity of <math id="S5.p3.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. By the same argument used in
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, p. 232]</cite>, the metric <math id="S5.p3.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> extends smoothly across
the <math id="S5.p3.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. By contrast, we obtain an edge-cone metric of cone-angle <math id="S5.p3.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> along
<math id="S5.p3.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, because our potential <math id="S5.p3.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> is asymptotic to the constant choice considered
in §<a href="#S4" title="4 Edges and Einstein Metrics ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
Since these edge-cone metrics satisfy
<math id="S5.p3.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{-}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{-}=0</annotation></semantics></math>, Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> tells us that
they also satisfy</p>

<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="S5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=1</annotation></semantics></math> case has some special features that make it particularly interesting. becomes</p>

</table>
<p id="S5.p4.3" class="ltx_p">where <span id="S5.p4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">ya</span> represents the hyperbolic distance from the point
<math id="S5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\sigma_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\sigma_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math> is a left-invariant orthonormal co-frame
for <math id="S5.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}=\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}=\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Remarkably, the alternative representative</p>
<table id="S5.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5.6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p4.4" class="ltx_p">of the conformal class is then Einstein, with Einstein constant <math id="S5.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=\frac{3}{2}\beta^{2}(2-\beta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=\frac{3}{2}\beta^{2}(2-\beta)</annotation></semantics></math>,
as follows from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, Equation (2.1)]</cite> or <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, §9]</cite>.
Demanding that <math id="S5.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> define a metric for all <math id="S5.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{ya}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>ya</mtext><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{ya}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> imposes the
constraint<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
          By contrast, when <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta&gt;2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta&gt;2</annotation></semantics></math>, restricting (<a href="#S5.E6" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>) to the <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-ball
<math id="footnote1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{ya}&lt;\tanh^{-1}(1-2/\beta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>ya</mtext><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msup><mi>tanh</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{ya}&lt;\tanh^{-1}(1-2/\beta)</annotation></semantics></math>
produces a family of complete self-dual Einstein metrics originally discovered by
Pedersen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>
that <math id="S5.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta&lt;2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta&lt;2</annotation></semantics></math>.
The resulting family of edge-cone metrics on <math id="S5.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>
of cone angle <math id="S5.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in(0,2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in(0,2)</annotation></semantics></math>, coincides with the
family constructed by Abreu <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, §5]</cite> by an entirely different method.
Notice that, as a special case of (<a href="#S5.E3" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>), these metrics satisfy</p>

<p id="S5.p4.5" class="ltx_p">whether we represent the conformal class by <math id="S5.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> or, when <math id="S5.p4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in(0,2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in(0,2)</annotation></semantics></math>, by <math id="S5.p4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="S5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is just the standard Fubini-Study metric
on <math id="S5.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. On the other hand, the <math id="S5.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to 2</annotation></semantics></math> limits
of <math id="S5.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{g}</annotation></semantics></math> give us
other celebrated metrics. For example, introducing the new radial coordinate
<math id="S5.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{r}=\sqrt{\coth\text{ya}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔯</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>coth</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mtext>ya</mtext></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{r}=\sqrt{\coth\text{ya}}</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>

<p id="S5.p5.2" class="ltx_p">which is the usual formula for the Eguchi-Hanson metric <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, a celebrated
complete self-dual Einstein metric on the manifold <math id="S5.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="TS^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">TS^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>; however,
(<a href="#S5.E8" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.8</span></a>) has arisen here as a metric on <math id="S5.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SU}(2)\times(1,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SU}(2)\times(1,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>
rather than on <math id="S5.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(3)\times(1,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(3)\times(1,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>, so this version of Eguchi-Hanson is actually
actually a branched double cover of the usual one, ramified along the zero section
of <math id="S5.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="TS^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">TS^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
On the other hand, after introducing a new radial coordinate <math id="S5.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{r}=\beta^{-1}\text{ya}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔯</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>ya</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{r}=\beta^{-1}\text{ya}</annotation></semantics></math>,
the point-wise coordinate limit</p>

<p id="S5.p5.3" class="ltx_p">is the Taub-NUT metric <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>,
a complete non-flat hyper-Kähler metric on <math id="S5.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Similarly, by
choosing suitable sequence of centers <math id="S5.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{p_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{p_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and conformal rescalings,
there are <math id="S5.p5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> limits of our conformal metrics on <math id="S5.p5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> which converge to</p>

<p id="S5.p5.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.p5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{dx}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐝𝐱</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{dx}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Euclidean metric on <math id="S5.p5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, the harmonic function</p>

</table>
<p id="S5.p5.5" class="ltx_p">is expressed in terms of the Euclidean distances <math id="S5.p5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{r}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝔯</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{r}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>
from the <math id="S5.p5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{p}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{p}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, and where <math id="S5.p5.m21" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="d\tilde{\Theta}=\star d\tilde{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">⋆</mo><mi>d</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>V</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\tilde{\Theta}=\star d\tilde{V}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The metric (<a href="#S5.E9" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.9</span></a>) is a famous gravitational instanton called the
multi-Taub-NUT metric <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">If we are cavalier about interchanging integrals and limits, these obseravtions
provide some interesting information regarding the above gravitational instantons.
For example, the standard Eguchi-Hanson space
<math id="S5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{EH}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{EH}}</annotation></semantics></math> should satisfy</p>
<table id="S5.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{EH}}|W_{+}|^{2}d\mu=\lim_{\beta\to 2^{-}}\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2+\beta^{2}}{3}\right)=1" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0.1389em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{12\pi^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{EH}}|W_{+}|^{2}d\mu=\lim_{\beta\to 2^{-}}\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2+\beta^{2}}{3}\right)=1</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p6.2" class="ltx_p">with respect to the orientation for which <math id="S5.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{-}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{-}=0</annotation></semantics></math>;
here the factor of <math id="S5.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> stems from the fact that <math id="S5.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{EH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{EH}</annotation></semantics></math> is a
<math id="S5.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-quotient of
<math id="S5.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}-\{p\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}-\{p\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Because the <math id="S5.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{-}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathring{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>̊</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathring{r}</annotation></semantics></math> pieces of the curvature
tensor <math id="S5.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> all vanish for <math id="S5.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{EH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{EH}</annotation></semantics></math>, the <math id="S5.p6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm squared of the
curvature of the Eguchi-Hanson instanton should therefore be given by</p>

<p id="S5.p6.4" class="ltx_p">when oriented so that <math id="S5.p6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{-}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{-}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, the <math id="S5.p6.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm squared of the

will have</p>

</table>
<p id="S5.p6.6" class="ltx_p">All of these interchanges of integrals and limits can in fact be rigorously justified
by a careful application of the the dominated convergence theorem.
Rather than presenting all the tedious details, however, we will instead simply
double-check these answers later, using a more direct method.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The self-dual Einstein edge-cone metrics on <math id="S5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> given by
(<a href="#S5.E6" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>)
are invariant under the action of <math id="S5.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S5.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}=\mathbb{C}^{2}\cup{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}=\mathbb{C}^{2}\cup{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, there is a remarkable second family of self-dual Einstein edge-cone metrics
on <math id="S5.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> which are invariant under a different action of
<math id="S5.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S5.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, namely the action of
<math id="S5.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(3)=\mathbf{SU}(2)/{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(3)=\mathbf{SU}(2)/{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S5.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> gotten by thinking
of it as the projective space of <math id="S5.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{C}\otimes{\mathbb{R}}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{C}\otimes{\mathbb{R}}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.
These metrics, which were
discovered by Hitchin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. The starting point of Hitchin’s investigation
was a reduction, due to Tod <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>,
of the self-dual Einstein equations with <math id="S5.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math>
symmetry to an ordinary differential equation belonging to the Painlevé VI family.
He then finds a specific family of solutions depending on an integer <math id="S5.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\geq 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\geq 3</annotation></semantics></math>
which have the property that the corresponding twistor spaces are (typically singular) algebraic
varieties, and then shows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, Proposition 5]</cite> that the resulting Einstein manifold compactifies as an edge-cone metric on <math id="S5.p7.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> of cone angle <math id="S5.p7.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\pi/(k-2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\pi/(k-2)</annotation></semantics></math>; he phrases this assertion
in terms of the
<math id="S5.p7.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-quotient of this metric by complex conjugation, which is then an orbifold metric on <math id="S5.p7.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>
with an edge-cone singularity of cone-angle <math id="S5.p7.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi/(k-2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi/(k-2)</annotation></semantics></math> along a Veronese <math id="S5.p7.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{RP}^{2}\subset S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{RP}^{2}\subset S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
When
<math id="S5.p7.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1</annotation></semantics></math>, Hitchin’s metric is just the Fubini-Study metric, while for <math id="S5.p7.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=2</annotation></semantics></math>
it is just a branched double cover of the standard metric on <math id="S5.p7.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The corresponding solutions of Painlevé VI can be explicitly expressed in terms
of elliptic functions, and Hitchin observes in a later paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, Remark 2, p. 79]</cite>
that, in principle,
solutions for non-integer <math id="S5.p7.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> should also give
rise to a self-dual Einstein edge-cone metrics on
<math id="S5.p7.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, although he does not try to determine precisely which cone angles
<math id="S5.p7.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\beta</annotation></semantics></math>
can
actually arise in this way. However, since <math id="S5.p7.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{RP}^{2}\subset{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{RP}^{2}\subset{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is totally real,
Proposition <a href="#S2.Thmprop2" title="Proposition 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> is perfectly adapted to the study of Hitchin’s self-dual edge-cone
metrics, and tells
us that they necessarily satisfy</p>
<table id="S5.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="S5.p7.2" class="ltx_p">We thus see that the constraint <math id="S5.p7.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\leq 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\leq 2</annotation></semantics></math>, corresponding to <math id="S5.p7.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\geq 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\geq 3</annotation></semantics></math>,
is both natural and unavoidable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="S5.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math>-action on <math id="S5.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> which preserves Hitchin’s metrics
has two <math id="S5.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional orbits, namely the <math id="S5.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{RP}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{RP}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> where the edge-cone singularity occurs,
and a conic <math id="S5.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C\subset{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C\subset{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> where the metric is smooth; in the
<math id="S5.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}={\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}={\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> model,
<math id="S5.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> projects to another Veronese <math id="S5.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{RP}^{2}=C/{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{RP}^{2}=C/{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Hitchin now normalizes his metrics so that <math id="S5.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> has area <math id="S5.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> for each
<math id="S5.p8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, and asks what happens when <math id="S5.p8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=2/(k-2)\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=2/(k-2)\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>. He then shows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, Proposition 6]</cite>
that this
<math id="S5.p8.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> limit is precisely the Atiyah-Hitchin gravitational instanton.
Here we need to be rather precise, because there are really two different versions of the
Atiyah-Hitchin instanton.
The better known version, which we shall call <math id="S5.p8.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{AH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{AH}</annotation></semantics></math>, was constructed
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> as the moduli space <math id="S5.p8.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{0}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{0}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of solutions of the <math id="S5.p8.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math> Bogomolny
monopole equations on <math id="S5.p8.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> with magnetic charge <math id="S5.p8.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> and
fixed center of mass. With this convention, <math id="S5.p8.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{AH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{AH}</annotation></semantics></math> is diffeomorphic to a
tubular neighborhood of the Veronese <math id="S5.p8.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{RP}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{RP}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S5.p8.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so
has fundamental group <math id="S5.p8.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Its universal cover <math id="S5.p8.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}</annotation></semantics></math>
is therefore also a gravitational instanton, and is diffeomorphic to a tubular neighborhood
of a conic <math id="S5.p8.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S5.p8.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>; thus, <math id="S5.p8.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}</annotation></semantics></math> is diffeomorphic both to
<math id="S5.p8.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}-\mathbb{RP}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}-\mathbb{RP}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and to the <math id="S5.p8.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{O}}(4)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{O}}(4)</annotation></semantics></math> line bundle
over <math id="S5.p8.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. If we regard Htichin’s metrics as edge-cone metrics on <math id="S5.p8.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},\mathbb{RP}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>,
he then shows that they converge to
<math id="S5.p8.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S5.p8.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>.
Interchanging limits and integration as before thus leads us to expect that</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

</table>
<p id="S5.p8.2" class="ltx_p">so that</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5.13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p8.3" class="ltx_p">and hence that</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

</table>
<p id="S5.p8.4" class="ltx_p">While this argument can again be made rigorous using the dominated convergence theorem,
we will instead simply double-check these answers
by a second
method which fits into a beautiful general pattern.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p9.1" class="ltx_p">So far, we have been using the signature formula (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.2 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) to compute the
<math id="S5.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-norm of the self-dual Weyl curvature for interesting edge-cone metrics,
and then, by a limiting process, have inferred the <math id="S5.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-norm of the Riemann curvature
for various
gravitational instantons, as <math id="S5.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{+}</annotation></semantics></math> is the only non-zero piece of the curvature
tensor for such spaces. However, we could have instead proceeded by considering the Gauss-Bonnet
formula (<a href="#S2.E1" title="In Theorem 2.1 ‣ 2 Curvature Integrals and Topology ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>) for edge-cone metrics. In this case, we have</p>
<table id="S5.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{\beta\to 0}\int_{M}\left[|\mathcal{R}|^{2}-|\mathring{r}|^{2}\right]d\mu=8\pi^{2}\lim_{\beta\to stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.052em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{\beta\to 0}\int_{M}\left[|\mathcal{R}|^{2}-|\mathring{r}|^{2}\right]d\mu=8\pi^{2}\lim_{\beta\to 0}\left[\chi(M)-(1-\beta)\chi(\Sigma)\right]=8\pi^{2}\chi(M-\Sigma)~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p9.2" class="ltx_p">Since the limit metric is Einstein, we thus expect any gravitational instanton
<math id="S5.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> obtained as a <math id="S5.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> limit to satisfy</p>
<table id="S5.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\int_{X}|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi(X)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_{X}|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi(X)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5.15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p9.3" class="ltx_p">because the underlying manifold of the instanton is <math id="S5.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=M-\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X=M-\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.
For example, the simply-connected Atiyah-Hitchin space <math id="S5.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}</annotation></semantics></math>
deform-retracts to <math id="S5.p9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so has Euler characteristic <math id="S5.p9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>; thus,
its total squared curvature should, as previously inferred, be <math id="S5.p9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\pi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\pi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Similarly, the Taub-NUT metric lives on the contractible space <math id="S5.p9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, which has Euler
characteristic <math id="S5.p9.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>, and so is expected to have <math id="S5.p9.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\int|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
in agreement with our previous inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p10.1" class="ltx_p">These same answers can be obtained in a
direct and
rigorous manner by
means of the Gauss-Bonnet theorem with boundary.
Indeed, if <math id="S5.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Y,g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Y,g)</annotation></semantics></math> is any compact oriented Riemannian
<math id="S5.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold-with-boundary, this result tells us</p>
<table id="S5.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">det</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>♊</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>♊</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">𝒶</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi(Y)=\frac{1}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{Y}\Big(|{\mathcal{R}}|^{2}-|\mathring{r}|^{2}\Big)\mu_{g}+\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\int_{\partial Y}\Big[2\det(\gemini)+\langle\gemini,\hat{\mathcal{R}}\rangle\Big]d{\zap a}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5.16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p10.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gemini" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>♊</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gemini</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d{\zap a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">𝒶</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d{\zap a}</annotation></semantics></math> are the
the second fundamental form and volume <math id="S5.p10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-form of the boundary <math id="S5.p10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial Y</annotation></semantics></math>,
is the of the boundary, and <math id="S5.p10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the symmetric tensor field on
<math id="S5.p10.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial Y</annotation></semantics></math> gotten by restricting the ambient curvature tensor <math id="S5.p10.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math>
and then
using the <math id="S5.p10.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional Hodge star operator
to identify <math id="S5.p10.m11" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\odot^{2}\Lambda^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot^{2}\Lambda^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p10.m12" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\odot^{2}\Lambda^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot^{2}\Lambda^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> on this <math id="S5.p10.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold.
One can prove (<a href="#S5.E16" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.16</span></a>) simply by following Chern’s proof of the
generalized Gauss-Bonnet theorem, using Stokes theorem to count
the zeroes, with multiplicities, of a generic vector field on <math id="S5.p10.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> that is an outward pointing
normal field along <math id="S5.p10.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial Y</annotation></semantics></math>. The proof in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> then goes through without changes, except that
there is now a non-trivial contribution due to <math id="S5.p10.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial Y</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p11.1" class="ltx_p">The best-known class of gravitational instantons consists of
ALE (Asymptotically Locally Euclidean) spaces. For such a space <math id="S5.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>, there is
a compact set <math id="S5.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S5.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X-K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X-K</annotation></semantics></math> is diffeomorphic to <math id="S5.p11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{R}}^{4}-B)/\Gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{R}}^{4}-B)/\Gamma</annotation></semantics></math>
for some finite subgroup <math id="S5.p11.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma\subset\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma\subset\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math>, in such a manner that
the metric is given by</p>
<table id="S5.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{jk}=\delta_{jk}+O(\mathsf{r}^{-2})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{jk}=\delta_{jk}+O(\mathsf{r}^{-2})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
