</table>
<p id="S5.p11.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.p11.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝗋</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Euclidean radius, with coordinate derivatives
<math id="S5.p11.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial^{k}g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mo>∂</mo><mi>k</mi></msup><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial^{k}g</annotation></semantics></math> commensurately falling off like <math id="S5.p11.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}^{-2-k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}^{-2-k}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In particular, a ball of radius <math id="S5.p11.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝗋</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}</annotation></semantics></math> has <math id="S5.p11.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-volume <math id="S5.p11.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim\mathsf{r}^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\mathsf{r}^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and the Riemannian curvature falls off like <math id="S5.p11.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{R}|\sim\mathsf{r}^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{R}|\sim\mathsf{r}^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Moreover, the hypersurface <math id="S5.p11.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}=\text{const}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝗋</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>const</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}=\text{const}</annotation></semantics></math> has <math id="S5.p11.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-volume <math id="S5.p11.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim\mathsf{r}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\mathsf{r}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>
and <math id="S5.p11.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\gemini|\sim\mathsf{r}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>♊</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\gemini|\sim\mathsf{r}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If we let <math id="S5.p11.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y\subset X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y\subset X</annotation></semantics></math> be the region <math id="S5.p11.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}\leq C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝗋</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}\leq C</annotation></semantics></math> and then
let <math id="S5.p11.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, we thus see that the only significant boundary contribution
in (<a href="#S5.E16" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.16</span></a>) comes from the <math id="S5.p11.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\det\gemini" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">det</mo><mi>♊</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\det\gemini</annotation></semantics></math> term. In the limit,
it is thus easy to show that the boundary terms just
equals <math id="S5.p11.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/|\Gamma|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/|\Gamma|</annotation></semantics></math> times the corresponding integral for the
standard <math id="S5.p11.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-sphere <math id="S5.p11.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus, any ALE instanton satisfies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite></p>
<table id="S5.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\int_{X}|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\left(\chi(X)-\frac{1}{|\Gamma|}\right)~." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="0.052em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_{X}|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\left(\chi(X)-\frac{1}{|\Gamma|}\right)~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S5.p11.3" class="ltx_p">For example, when <math id="S5.p11.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is the Eguchi-Hanson instanton <math id="S5.p11.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{EH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{EH}</annotation></semantics></math>,
<math id="S5.p11.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi=2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p11.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\Gamma|=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\Gamma|=2</annotation></semantics></math>, so the total squared curvature is <math id="S5.p11.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12\pi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12\pi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
as previously predicted by (<a href="#S5.E10" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.10</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p12.1" class="ltx_p">The Taub-NUT space is the prototypical example of an asymptotically
locally flat (ALF) gravitational instanton.
For such spaces, the volume of a large ball has <math id="S5.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-volume <math id="S5.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim\mathsf{r}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\mathsf{r}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>,
while curvature falls off like <math id="S5.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>. The hypersurface <math id="S5.p12.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}=\text{const}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝗋</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>const</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}=\text{const}</annotation></semantics></math>
has <math id="S5.p12.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-volume <math id="S5.p12.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim\mathsf{r}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\mathsf{r}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S5.p12.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\gemini|\sim\mathsf{r}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>♊</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\gemini|\sim\mathsf{r}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p12.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\det\gemini\sim\mathsf{r}^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">det</mo><mi>♊</mi></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\det\gemini\sim\mathsf{r}^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus the boundary contribution in (<a href="#S5.E16" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.16</span></a>) tends to zero as <math id="S5.p12.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{r}\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝗋</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{r}\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, and
any ALF instanton therefore satisfies the simpler formula <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite></p>
<table id="S5.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\int_{X}|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi(X)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_{X}|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi(X)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5.18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p12.2" class="ltx_p">previously seen in (<a href="#S5.E15" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.15</span></a>).
For example, the Taub-NUT instanton has <math id="S5.p12.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi=1</annotation></semantics></math>, so its total squared curvature
<math id="S5.p12.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8\pi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\pi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, as predicted by (<a href="#S5.E11" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.11</span></a>). The Atiyah-Hitchin gravitational instanton is also
ALF; in fact, it is
asymptotic to Taub-NUT with a negative NUT parameter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. Thus <math id="S5.p12.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}</annotation></semantics></math>, with an Euler characteristic of <math id="S5.p12.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>, has total squared curvature <math id="S5.p12.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\pi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\pi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
while its <math id="S5.p12.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-quotient <math id="S5.p12.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{AH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{AH}</annotation></semantics></math>, with an Euler characteristic of <math id="S5.p12.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>, has
has total squared curvature <math id="S5.p12.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8\pi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\pi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that these conclusions coincide
with the predictions of (<a href="#S5.E13" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.13</span></a>) and (<a href="#S5.E14" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.14</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p13.1" class="ltx_p">A classification of complete hyper-Kähler ALE <math id="S5.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds was given by
Kronheimer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>;
up to deformation, they are in one-to-one correspondence with
the Dynkin diagrams of type <math id="S5.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.p13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, the
Dynkin diagram <math id="S5.p13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the
Eguchi-Hanson metric, and, more generally,
the Dynkin diagrams <math id="S5.p13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to
the multi-Eguchi-Hanson metrics independently discovered by
Hitchin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> and by Gibbons-Hawking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. Each Dynkin diagram
represents a discrete subgroup <math id="S5.p13.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S5.p13.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SU}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SU}(2)</annotation></semantics></math>, and these groups are
then realized as the fundamental group of the <math id="S5.p13.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional boundary
at infinity of the corresponding <math id="S5.p13.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold.
The diagram also elegantly encodes the diffeotype of the corresponding <math id="S5.p13.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold,
which is obtained by plumbing together copies of <math id="S5.p13.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="TS^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">TS^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, with one <math id="S5.p13.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-sphere
for each node, and with edges of the diagram indicating which pairs of <math id="S5.p13.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-spheres
meet. In particular, the number <math id="S5.p13.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> of nodes in any given diagram is the second Betti number
<math id="S5.p13.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of the instanton, which consequently has <math id="S5.p13.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi=k+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi=k+1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p14.1" class="ltx_p">For each diagram of type <math id="S5.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S5.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>, there is also an associated ALF instanton.
These ALF partners
are diffeomorphic to the corresponding ALE instantons, but their geometry at infinity
resembles Taub-NUT<math id="S5.p14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="/\Gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">/\Gamma</annotation></semantics></math> instead of a Euclidean
quotient <math id="S5.p14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{4}/\Gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{4}/\Gamma</annotation></semantics></math>.
In the <math id="S5.p14.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> cases, these spaces are just the multi-Taub-NUT metrics of (<a href="#S5.E9" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.9</span></a>),
with
<math id="S5.p14.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=k+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=k+1</annotation></semantics></math> centers; our heuristic calculation (<a href="#S5.E12" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.12</span></a>)
of their total squared curvature thus confirmed by (<a href="#S5.E18" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.18</span></a>), since these spaces
have <math id="S5.p14.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi=n</annotation></semantics></math>.
The <math id="S5.p14.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> metrics were constructed explicitly
by Cherkis and Hitchin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, building on earlier existence arguments
of Cherkis and Kapustin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. The fact that these metrics really are
ALF follows from results due to Gibbons-Manton <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> and Bielawski <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> gives a compilation of the total squared curvature of these important spaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Of course, several of the
gravitational instantons
we have discussed do not appear on Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>;
the Taub-NUT space <math id="S5.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{TN}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝕋</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{TN}</annotation></semantics></math> and the Atiyah-Hitchin manifolds <math id="S5.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{AH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{AH}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S5.p15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\mathbb{AH}}</annotation></semantics></math> are nowhere to be found. Of course, one might decree <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>
that <math id="S5.p15.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{TN}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝕋</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{TN}</annotation></semantics></math> is the ALF entry across from the fictitious diagram <math id="S5.p15.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>,
or that <math id="S5.p15.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{AH}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔸</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℍ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{AH}</annotation></semantics></math> is the ALF entry associated with the make-believe
diagram <math id="S5.p15.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>; but to us, this is less interesting than the general point that
that <math id="S5.p15.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\int|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi</annotation></semantics></math> for complete Ricci-flat <math id="S5.p15.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds with ALF asymptotics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p16.1" class="ltx_p">There is a large realm of gravitational instantons which
have slower volume growth, but still have finite topological type.
Cherkis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_citation ltx_ref_self">cheralh</span>]</cite> has proposed sorting these into two classes: the ALG
spaces, with at least quadratic volume growth, and the ALH instantons,
with sub-quadratic volume growth. For example,
Tian and Yau <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> constructed
hyper-Kähler metrics on the complement of an anti-canonical divisor on any
del Pezzo surface; these metrics have volume growth <math id="S5.p16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim\mathsf{r}^{4/3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><msup><mi>𝗋</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\mathsf{r}^{4/3}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so
are of ALH type. For these examples, one has enough control at infinity
to see that the boundary term in (<a href="#S5.E16" title="In 5 Edges and Instantons ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.16</span></a>) becomes negligeable at large radii, so that
the pattern <math id="S5.p16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\int|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int|\mathcal{R}|^{2}d\mu=8\pi^{2}\chi</annotation></semantics></math>
continues to hold. Presumably, this pattern will also turn out to hold for
all gravitational instantons of type ALG and ALH.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p17.1" class="ltx_p">Many gravitational instantons do seem to arise as
limits of edge-cone Einstein metrics. For instance,
the results of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> strongly suggest that the ALH
examples of Tian-Yau are
<math id="S5.p17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>
limits of Kähler-Einstein edge-cone metrics;
proving this, however, would entail first establishing
a suitable lower bound for the <math id="S5.p17.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-energy. It would obviously be
interesting to prove the existence of
sequences of Einstein edge-cone metrics which tend to other known examples of gravitational
instantons.
On the other hand, one might hope to construct new examples of
gravitational instantons as
Gromov-Hausdorff limits of suitable sequences of
<math id="S5.p17.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional Einstein edge-cone manifolds. While some features of
weak convergence for smooth Einstein metrics
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_citation ltx_ref_self">andprior</span>, <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_citation ltx_ref_self">cheeti</span>]</cite> may carry over
with little change, it seems likely that the introduction of
edge-cone singularities may involve some serious
technical difficulties. Our hope is that the regime of
small <math id="S5.p17.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> will nonetheless prove to
be manageable, and that the theory that emerges will lead to
new insights concerning
precisely which gravitational instantons arise as <math id="S5.p17.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> limits of Einstein spaces
with edge-cone singularities.</p>
</div>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Appendix</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The proof outlined in §<a href="#S3" title="3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> involves the use of the signature theorem for orbifolds. We
will now
indicate how this can be deduced from the theory of transversally elliptic operators
developed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. For further details, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> be a compact manifold equipped with the action of a compact Lie group <math id="A1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A differential operator <math id="A1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> between vector bundles on <math id="A1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is said to be <span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">transversally elliptic</span> if it is <math id="A1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-invariant, and its restriction to any submanifold transverse to a <math id="A1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-orbit is elliptic.
A trivial but important example arises when <math id="A1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> acts freely on <math id="A1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>, so that <math id="A1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X/\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X/\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is itself a manifold; in this case, a transversally elliptic operator is essentially just
an elliptic operator on <math id="A1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X/\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X/\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>. For us, the case of primary interest occurs when the action
of <math id="A1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> has only finite isotropy groups. In this case, <math id="A1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X/\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X/\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is an orbifold.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The index of such a transversally elliptic operator <math id="A1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>
is an invariant distribution on <math id="A1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>. Equivalently, the index is given by an infinite series</p>
<table id="A1.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ind(D)=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\rho}\chi_{\rho}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ind</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>λ</mi></munder><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>χ</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ind(D)=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\rho}\chi_{\rho}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(A.1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> runs over the irreducible representations of <math id="A1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi_{\rho}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>χ</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi_{\rho}</annotation></semantics></math> is the character of <math id="A1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and the multiplicities <math id="A1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\rho}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\rho}</annotation></semantics></math> do not grow too fast.
If <math id="A1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> is fully elliptic, then the sum in (<a href="#A1.E1" title="In Appendix A Appendix ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>) is finite. In general, however, it may be infinite; for example, if <math id="A1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X=\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is equipped with the left action of <math id="A1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> on itself, and if <math id="A1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> is the zero operator, then <math id="A1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\lambda}=\dim\chi_{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>λ</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">dim</mo><msub><mi>χ</mi><mi>λ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\lambda}=\dim\chi_{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math> and (<a href="#A1.E1" title="In Appendix A Appendix ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>)
just becomes the Peter-Weyl decomposition of <math id="A1.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}(\mathbf{G})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐆</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}(\mathbf{G})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A general procedure for computing the index of
<math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> is described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. Some of the key points are:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="A1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(i)</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The distribution
<math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ind(D)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ind</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ind(D)</annotation></semantics></math> only depends <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, Theorem (2.6)]</cite>
on the <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-theory class of the symbol of <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> in the group <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{\mathbf{G}}(T^{*}_{\mathbf{G}}X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>𝐆</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mi>𝐆</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{\mathbf{G}}(T^{*}_{\mathbf{G}}X)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{*}_{\mathbf{G}}X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mi>𝐆</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{*}_{\mathbf{G}}X</annotation></semantics></math> is the subspace of the cotangent bundle <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{*}X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{*}X</annotation></semantics></math> annihilated by the Lie algebra of <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e. “transverse” to the <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-orbits).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(ii)</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The distribution
<math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ind(D)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ind</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ind(D)</annotation></semantics></math> is supported <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, Theorem (4.6)]</cite>
by the conjugacy classes of all elements of <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> that have fixed points in <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(iii)</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore,
<math id="A1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ind(D)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ind</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ind(D)</annotation></semantics></math> is covariant <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, Theorems (4.1) and (4.3)]</cite>
with respect to embeddings <math id="A1.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐆</mi><mo stretchy="false">↪</mo><mi>𝐇</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{H}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\hookrightarrow Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">↪</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\hookrightarrow Z</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(iv)</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a connected Lie group <math id="A1.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>,
computation of <math id="A1.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ind(D)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ind</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ind(D)</annotation></semantics></math> can be reduced <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, Theorem (4.2)]</cite>
to the case of a maximal torus <math id="A1.I1.i4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐓</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, replacing <math id="A1.I1.i4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="A1.I1.i4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\times\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐓</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\times\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(v)</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="A1.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> has only finite isotropy groups, the transverse signature operator is transversally elliptic. Its index equals the signature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, Theorem (10.3)]</cite>
of the rational homology manifold <math id="A1.I1.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X/\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X/\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(vi)</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If, in (<a href="#A1.I1.i5" title="item v ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">v</span></a>), <math id="A1.I1.i6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is a torus,
then the signature of <math id="A1.I1.i6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X/\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X/\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> can be expressed in cohomological terms involving the (finitely many) fixed point sets <math id="A1.I1.i6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A1.I1.i6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}\in\mathbf{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝐓</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}\in\mathbf{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. This formula coincides with the Lefschetz Theorem formula (3.9) of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i7" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(vii)</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using (<a href="#A1.I1.i4" title="item iv ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">iv</span></a>), the signature formula (<a href="#A1.I1.i6" title="item vi ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">vi</span></a>) extends to all <math id="A1.I1.i7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> by using standard results about the flag manifold <math id="A1.I1.i7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐆</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐓</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In the special case when <math id="A1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dim X=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">dim</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dim X=4</annotation></semantics></math>, the signature formula for an orbifold is just equation (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), which is what we need in this paper. However the general theory also applies to the higher-dimensional case, when <math id="A1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dim X=4k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">dim</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dim X=4k</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">It remains to explain how the signature theorem for an (oriented) orbifold <math id="A1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> can be derived from this theory of transversally elliptic operators. In fact, we only need the special case when <math id="A1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=X/\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=X/\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is the quotient of a manifold by a compact group <math id="A1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math> acting with only finite isotropy groups. The key observation (not widely known, but used already in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>) is that the oriented frame bundle of any oriented
orbifold is a smooth manifold <math id="A1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>; we can thus just take <math id="A1.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X=P</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A1.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐆</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math>. We just need to to verify that <math id="A1.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> is a manifold,
and that <math id="A1.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math> acts on it with only finite isotropy.
This problem is essentially local, we may
assume that <math id="A1.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\Gamma\backslash U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">\</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\Gamma\backslash U</annotation></semantics></math>, where the finite group
<math id="A1.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma\subset\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma\subset\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math> acts on <math id="A1.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U\approx{\mathbb{R}}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>≈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U\approx{\mathbb{R}}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> by left multiplication;
moreover, there is a trivialization
<math id="A1.p7.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(U)\cong U\times\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(U)\cong U\times\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math> such a manner that
<math id="A1.p7.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma</annotation></semantics></math> acts freely on <math id="A1.p7.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math> on the left, thus commuting with the natural
right action by <math id="A1.p7.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math>. We now see that <math id="A1.p7.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(M)=\Gamma\backslash P(U)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">\</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(M)=\Gamma\backslash P(U)</annotation></semantics></math>
is therefore a manifold, and that
<math id="A1.p7.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=P(M)/\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=P(M)/\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math>. Furthermore,
every isotropy group of the
<math id="A1.p7.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math> action on <math id="A1.p7.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(M)</annotation></semantics></math>
is now a subgroup
of some isotropy group for the right action of <math id="A1.p7.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math> on
<math id="A1.p7.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{SO}(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">\</mo><mrow><mi>𝐒𝐎</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{SO}(n)</annotation></semantics></math>,
and so is conjugate to a subgroup of <math id="A1.p7.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Much of our discussion generalizes nicely to higher dimensions.
The <math id="A1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>-signature theorem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, (6.12)]</cite>
gives an explicit cohomological formula for the signature
<math id="A1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau({\zap g},X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau({\zap g},X)</annotation></semantics></math>, for any <math id="A1.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\zap g}\in\mathbf{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝐆</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\zap g}\in\mathbf{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, in terms of its fixed point set <math id="A1.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="A1.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y=X^{\zap g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℊ</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y=X^{\zap g}</annotation></semantics></math> is of codimension <math id="A1.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> with
normal cone angle <math id="A1.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=2\pi/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=2\pi/p</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> an integer, the contribution of <math id="A1.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> becomes</p>
<table id="A1.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\{2^{2k-1}\mathscr{L}(Y)\coth(\dfrac{y+i\beta}{2})\right\}[Y]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℒ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>coth</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{2^{2k-1}\mathscr{L}(Y)\coth(\dfrac{y+i\beta}{2})\right\}[Y]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(A.2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p8.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathscr{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathscr{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is the stable characteristic class given by</p>
<table id="A1.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathscr{L}=\sum\mathscr{L}_{r}(p)=\prod\dfrac{x_{i}/2}{\tanh x_{i}/2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℒ</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathscript">ℒ</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>tanh</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathscr{L}=\sum\mathscr{L}_{r}(p)=\prod\dfrac{x_{i}/2}{\tanh x_{i}/2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(A.3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p8.3" class="ltx_p">which is essentially the Hirzebruch <math id="A1.p8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>-series with <math id="A1.p8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x/2</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A1.p8.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.
Here, <math id="A1.p8.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the first Chern class of the normal bundle of <math id="A1.p8.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y\subset X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y\subset X</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The “defect” contribution of <math id="A1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> to the signature
<math id="A1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(X)</annotation></semantics></math> is given by replacing <math id="A1.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="A1.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\leq r&lt;p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\leq r&lt;p</annotation></semantics></math> in (<a href="#A1.E2" title="In Appendix A Appendix ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>),
summing over <math id="A1.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> and dividing by <math id="A1.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. This gives an explicit polynomial in <math id="A1.p9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> and the Pontrjagin classes of <math id="A1.p9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>, depending on <math id="A1.p9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>. In the <math id="A1.p9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1</annotation></semantics></math> case, where <math id="A1.p9.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dim X=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">dim</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dim X=4</annotation></semantics></math>, we recover the formula (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3 Indices and Orbifolds ‣ Curvature, Cones, and Characteristic Numbers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, one can extend this formula to all <math id="A1.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> , and thereby
compute the signature defect due to any edge-cone singularity along <math id="A1.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>.
To do this, we proceed as before, first obtaining a formula for
rational values of <math id="A1.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=q/p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=q/p</annotation></semantics></math>, and then extending it to all real values by continuity.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Acknowledgements.</span> The authors would both particularly
like to express their gratitude
to the Simons Center for
Geometry and Physics for its hospitality during the Fall semester of 2011,
during which time this project began to take shape.
They would also like to thank fellow Simons Center visitors Nigel Hitchin and
Sergey Cherkis for many useful discussions of gravitational instantons and related topics.
The second author would also like to thank Rafe Mazzeo and Xiuxiong Chen for a number of
helpful suggestions.</p>
